How the score is built

Each company’s latest quarter is scored 0–100 on five weighted pillars: revenue growth YoY (22%), operating profit growth YoY (26%), core net profit growth YoY (22%), operating margin change YoY (20%) and sequential momentum vs. the March quarter (10%). Each pillar is banded against absolute thresholds, not ranked against peers, so a weak quarter for the whole market stays a weak quarter here. Growth is only computed off a positive base — a percentage off a loss is meaningless — and sign flips are handled as events instead.

Exceptional items are stripped out

The profit pillar runs on core profit: net profit less extraordinary items, compared against the year‑ago quarter on the same basis. An asset sale is not an operating result. Where an exceptional item moves net profit by more than 20%, the company carries a one‑off marker — 121 companies this quarter — and the drawer shows the reported and core figures side by side. Turnaround and Disaster are set from the actual sign of the year‑ago profit, not inferred from a growth percentage.

Quality, shareholding, valuation

Quality reads Piotroski, ROCE, ROE and debt‑to‑equity, plus a direction term: whether ROCE is above or below where it stood a year ago (1,169 companies improving, 1,613 deteriorating). For banks and NBFCs, where debt is the raw material, return on assets takes the leverage slot. Shareholding scores the quarter’s change in the register: promoter action and net FII + DII flow at 50% each, less a pledge penalty; promoters rarely trade, so standing still is neutral, and a company institutions never owned is uncovered rather than abandoned. Valuation compares P/E to both the industry and the company’s own 5‑year median.

Two flags on the data itself

523 companies are SME‑platform listings — lighter reporting, thin volume, and a visibly rosier rating mix (19.5% Blockbuster against 11.7% on the main board). The Exclude SME chip removes them. Separately, 586 companies carry receivables above 1.75× their sector median; debtor days only mean something against the sector, since 90 days is routine in capital goods and alarming in food retail. Those carry a Stretched receivables filter — revenue that is not converting to cash.

“vs trend” is not the street

Screener’s expected‑quarter figures correlate 0.987 with the preceding quarter: they are a trend extrapolation, not analyst consensus. Beating them means the company beat its own run‑rate, which is worth knowing but is not an earnings surprise in the market sense. That is why this axis sits outside the score rather than inside it, and why the label reads “vs trend”. Coverage is 76% of the universe; the rest show No estimate.

Read it with these caveats

Source is a Screener.in export; figures are consolidated and in ₹ crore. 511 companies had not reported the June 2026 quarter when this was pulled — their latest result is March 2026 or older. They are hidden by default; the Reported this quarter chip brings them back, greyed, with their result date shown. Beyond that, the score reads reported numbers and cannot see a demerger or merger, so companies whose base year no longer exists (ITC’s hotels demerger, Siemens’ energy split) score against a base that is gone. Oil marketers swing on inventory losses and real estate on revenue recognition. A rating is a starting point for a read, not a verdict, and nothing here is investment advice.
